newsitem.title: GERMANY: Gene-altered soybean row may spill over into feeds.
newsitem.headline: Gene-altered soybean row may spill over into feeds.

text.p: Genetically-altered soybeans at the centre of a European furore may also damage the image of soymeal, which is a key protein source in the animal feed industry, German sources said on Thursday.
"There could be pressure from farmers on feed mixers and oil mills to label soymeal derived from these new soybeans, which would associate the meal with problems," a broker said.
"Grocery chains might demand meat products come from animals that were fed with biotechnology-free soymeal."
"It's early days, but I wouldn't rule it out because consumers are extremely sensitive to what happens in meat production after the experiences with the madcow crisis."
Environmental groups opposed to genetic engineering are coordinating a campaign against the import of genetically manipulated U.S. soybeans, citing possible health risks.
German and Dutch brokers said rape meal prices were firm on tight rapeseed supply while soymeal was cheaper, although unusual demand shifts either way could not be detected.

But Greenpeace activists in Hamburg said they would monitor where meal from the new beans was sent after it left the local oil mill Oelag, the first known processor of possibly altered U.S. new crop beans.
Having successfully weaned oil consumers off soy products, they were planning to exert pressure on meal buyers.
A feeds expert at farm union DBV said farmers did not doubt the new beans were safe but needed to appease their customers.
"Farmers, along with other consumers, must know what they are buying to be accountable to worried customers," he said.
"Feed containing genetically-altered organisms should be recognisable as such."
"In any case, we don't understand why U.S. suppliers cannot label non-modified beans to help us out."
Compound feed industry associaton FFMI in Bonn said current legislation did not provide for a separate labelling of meals from new and conventional beans as they were identical.
But managing director Hubert Grote said discussions with the farm ministry had revealed the position could change to respond to demands for practicable labelling.
German seed crushers last year produced 2.8 million tonnes of soymeal and 1.9 million tonnes of rapemeal.
In addition, some 1.9 million tonnes of ready soymeal were imported, out of a total 3.3 million tonnes of oilmeal imports.
